name: Maritime pine bark extract (Pycnogenol)

lead: Pycnogenol is a branded extract of French maritime pine bark rich in procyanidins, sold as an antioxidant supplement and mentioned for skin and melasma.
A Cochrane review found insufficient evidence for efficacy across the conditions it examined, and the sources reviewed hold no skin or melasma trial.

paras: Lab studies report free-radical scavenging and inhibition of matrix metalloproteinases by its metabolites, the basis for skin-ageing interest. Human skin effects have not been shown in the sources reviewed.
Safety is not covered in the sources reviewed. It is sold as a dietary supplement, not a drug.

lead: Pycnogenol is the trademarked name of a standardised extract of French maritime pine (Pinus pinaster) bark, composed mainly of proanthocyanidins (procyanidins, about 70%).[1][2] The term was coined in 1979 by chemist Jack Masquelier, who had extracted proanthocyanidins from pine bark.[2]

It is sold as an antioxidant supplement and is discussed in skin-care circles, including for pigmentation concerns such as melasma. Laboratory work reports free-radical scavenging and inhibition of matrix metalloproteinases by its metabolites.[3][4]

A Cochrane review, updated in 2020 and summarised on Wikipedia, examined uses including asthma, ADHD, blood pressure, osteoarthritis and cognition after brain injury, and found insufficient evidence of efficacy; meta-analyses have likewise found insufficient evidence for any disease.[2] The sources reviewed contain no skin or melasma trial.

paras: A 2002 review described a diverse pharmacology for the extract, covering antioxidant, anti-inflammatory and vascular actions identified in laboratory and clinical studies.[1] Metabolites of the extract showed antioxidant activity and inhibition of matrix metalloproteinases, enzymes involved in collagen breakdown, in a 2004 study, which is the basis of skin-related interest.[3] Related experiments found that pine-bark polyphenols reduced nitric oxide production and inflammatory signalling in macrophages and increased plasma antioxidant capacity.[5][6]
Pine bark extracts are also studied outside medicine, for example as natural preservatives in meat.[7]

Registered trials cover hypertension (UPBEAT, n=130), arm lymphedema after breast cancer (Phase 2, n=26), ADHD (two studies, n=32 and n=88), gum inflammation (n=90), traumatic brain injury (n=67), mild cognitive impairment and exercise fatigue.[8][9][10][11] The Cochrane review cited by Wikipedia found insufficient evidence for efficacy across the indications it examined.[2]
No studies on skin quality, wrinkles or melasma were found in the sources reviewed.

Masquelier is credited with extracting proanthocyanidins from European maritime pine bark and introducing the name Pycnogenol in 1979, reportedly inspired by an account of bark tea used by Jacques Cartier's expedition.[2]

timeline.event: Cochrane review update finds insufficient evidence for efficacy in the conditions examined.[2]
